title: When grief comes
hookLine: the eyes weep and the heart grieves, but we say only what pleases our Lord (Bukhari)
tomorrow: if Allah decides who heals, why bother with a doctor?

cards: A car in a hospital garage, engine off. A grandmother crying into her scarf, then wiping her face fast and saying alhamdulillah, as if she's been caught at something.
Tears can feel like a leak in faith, a thing to patch before anyone sees. In one hadith a companion seems to think so too. The Prophet's little son, Ibrahim, is dying, and the Prophet's eyes fill.
And Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, one of his close companions, asks him something odd. Two words, really. Even you?
A gentle note for parents: this story is about a child's death.

teach.b: Even you, Messenger of Allah? As if tears belonged to people with less faith. His answer, in Sahih al-Bukhari, was short: it is mercy.

teach.h: THE EYES WEEP, THE HEART GRIEVES.
teach.b: Then he said the line this whole day turns on: the eyes shed tears and the heart grieves, and we say only what pleases our Lord. And he spoke to his son by name: we are saddened by your parting, O Ibrahim.

teach.h: THE LINE IS AT THE TONGUE.
teach.b: The hadith does draw a line, just not where Abd al-Rahman expected. Not between crying and not crying. In other reports the Prophet warned against slapping faces and tearing clothes at a death; that's where the line sits.
The eyes may weep. The heart may ache. Those are mercy, he said, not weakness.
What stays guarded is the tongue: no words of protest against God, only what pleases Him.
Grief gets the eyes and the heart.
Trust gets the words. Both at once, in the same moment, from the same person, holding his son.

how: At a death, Muslims are free to cry; mourners are asked to avoid wailing and words of protest, and many say inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un and make du'a for the one who has died.

o: grief so deep it turns into anger at God
grief that lets tears fall and keeps its trust
a sadness strong faith is meant to stop

games.q: who said what — tap the pairs.
p: says only what pleases our Lord

s: crying at a death shows weak faith in Islam
the Prophet wept for his son Ibrahim and called the tears mercy.
the hadith draws its line at the tongue, not the eyes
the eyes weep, the heart grieves, and we say only what pleases our Lord.

games.q: at her father's funeral, a friend apologizes to you for crying and says she should be stronger. what does the hadith give you?
o: tears are mercy; even the Prophet wept for his son.
let it out today, then be strong for the family.
strong people grieve at home, not in front of others.
games.why: the Prophet cried openly, holding his son, and called it mercy. what he guarded was the tongue, not the eyes.

practice: If there's something nearby that belonged to someone you miss, or a photo on your phone, look at it. If no one comes to mind, think of any loss: a place, a season, a friendship.
Let your eyes do whatever they do, without stopping them. If you pray, let any words be ones that please your Lord; silence is fine too.

wordCard.voice: When grief comes: the eyes weep, the heart grieves, and the words stay with God. The Prophet called the tears mercy.

orig.note: Arabic: mercy. the Prophet's word for his own tears at his son's death (Bukhari).

carryVoice: Your line: weep, and trust. The same person can do both, in the same moment. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 1303 (Ibrahim's death: 'even you?'; 'it is mercy'; the eyes shed tears and the heart grieves)
Sahih al-Bukhari 1294 (not of us who slaps the cheeks and tears the clothes)
